key_insight: Parents and pediatric staff are more accepting of AI when the condition feels more severe, but trust drops when data sharing expands or AI conflicts with clinicians.
clinical_relevance: Pediatric AI tools may be more acceptable for treatment support than diagnosis, but successful adoption will depend on clear privacy protections, accuracy, and accountability.
method: Surveyed parents in two cohorts (n=198 and n=79) and pediatric healthcare professionals (n=33).
Compared AI acceptability across disease, diagnosis, and treatment scenarios.
Assessed predictors including data privacy preferences, AI knowledge, and perceived disease severity.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports statistical associations, including lower willingness with more liberal data privacy (p < .001) and higher willingness with greater perceived disease severity in the second parent cohort (β = .10, p = .013).
watch_item: Findings are preference-based and scenario-specific, so real-world use still needs validation in diverse pediatric settings with strong privacy safeguards.
paper_title: Acceptability of AI-applications in routine clinical care for children and adolescents: perspectives of parents and healthcare professionals
